title: Calibrating Africa’s green industrialization strategy, Part 1
body:
Africa’s green industrialization strategy must be calibrated to reflect the hard realities of today’s geoeconomic landscape.

Despite the continent’s abundant endowment of transition minerals, these resources have not translated into commensurate gains in domestic processing, manufacturing, or technological capability—as we demonstrate in our recent report (https://lnkd.in/eJUPe8hF). Instead, value capture has increasingly occurred outside the continent, most notably in China.

This moment therefore calls for a decisive recalibration of Africa’s green industrialization agenda. Again, the priority is not disengagement from dominant external partners, but strategic leverage—using Africa’s mineral endowments to negotiate technology transfer, co-investment, and regionally anchored processing hubs that support long-term structural transformation. Without such a shift, Africa risks underwriting the global green transition while remaining industrially peripheral to it.

Recalibrating this strategy requires moving beyond aspirational ideals toward policy conditions that are not only essential for repositioning Africa within the emerging green industrial order but also aligned with the region’s current realities. Among others, this includes:

- From partners to terms of engagement: Strategic engagement with external partners must move beyond partnership rhetoric toward enforceable terms. Clear value-addition benchmarks, co-investment in processing infrastructure, and credible technology transfer provisions should define access to Africa’s strategic minerals, not open-ended extraction rights.
- Industrial policy coherence: Building green industrial ecosystems requires disciplined coordination across ministries, development finance institutions, and regulators. Fragmented policy approaches will continue to undermine Africa’s ability to convert mineral endowments into industrial capabilities.
- Energy first, slogans later: Green industrialization without reliable, affordable, and scalable energy systems is a contradiction. Power sector reform, grid expansion, and industrial energy planning must precede—or at least move in lockstep with—ambitions for mineral processing and green manufacturing.
- Capability before complexity: Africa does not need to capture entire green value chains overnight. Strategic sequencing—starting with feasible processing stages and advancing through learning-by-doing—offers a more realistic, resilient, and politically sustainable pathway to industrial upgrading.
- Regionalize or remain marginal: The capital intensity and scale requirements of green industries exceed the capacity of most individual African economies. African countries must think regionally. A national strategic vision,

embedded and anchored in regional integration, is key.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD
